sentences.text: Unlike its relatives, the squamosal bone of Sunosuchus is notably narrow.
Fossil specimens include numerous teeth, a dorsal vertebra, vertebral centra, pelvic bones, parts of the fibula and tibia, metatarsals, and osteoderms from the ventral and neck regions.
The species Sunosuchus thailandicus is known only from a very robust lower jaw.
In this species, the tip of the jaw is spoon-shaped and wider than the section immediately behind it.
A newly discovered specimen suggests that S. thailandicus is distinct enough to warrant placement in its own genus, Chalawan.
S. junggarensis is the best known species, first described in 1996 from Late Jurassic deposits in the Junggar Basin of Xinjiang, China.
Material collected from Kyrgyzstan in the 1980s was not described until the year 2000.
S. shunanensis was described in 2005 from Middle Jurassic rocks in Zigong, Sichuan, China.
Sunosuchus thailandicus was originally described from northeastern Thailand in 1980.
The fauna found with Sunosuchus in Kyrgyzstan, including temnospondyl amphibians and xinjiangchelyid turtles, indicates freshwater environments.
However, the presence of marine hybodont sharks and dipnoans in Kyrgyzstan strata suggests the area was estuarine rather than entirely freshwater.
Sunosuchus was initially classified as a pholidosaurid due to its long, long-snouted jaws.
Despite similarities with pholidosaurs, Sunosuchus shares features that ally it with goniopholidids.
The animal is classified in the class Reptilia.
Sunosuchus lived from the Bajocian to the Tithonian stages, between 170.9 and 143.1 million years ago.
Fossils date from the Middle Jurassic to the Early Cretaceous, with possible Early Jurassic occurrences.
Fossils of Sunosuchus have been found in China, Kyrgyzstan, and Thailand and are Jurassic in age, though some may be Early Cretaceous.
The Kyrgyzstan material represents the westernmost record of Sunosuchus's geographic range.
The parent group of the genus Sunosuchus is Goniopholididae.
